page4_img_1.png.title: State pattern UML: Context (template), State (hook), ConcreteState implementations
page4_img_1.png.description: A UML-style diagram of the State pattern: a Context class (top-left) contains a field labeled "State state" and a method "Request()" that delegates to the State interface. To the right, a State box exposes "Handle()" and is shown as the superclass (triangle) of two subclasses, ConcreteStateA and ConcreteStateB, each with their own "Handle()". A dashed callout labeled "state->Handle()" emphasizes that Context forwards requests to the current State instance. The paper uses this figure to illustrate the 1-1-Connection metapattern mapping: Context = template, State = hook, and ConcreteState classes = implementations, a structural view relevant to the study of change-proneness.

page7_img_1.png.title: Mapping of design patterns to metapattern categories
page7_img_1.png.description: Two-column table that maps Pree’s metapattern categories (left column) to the corresponding Gang‑of‑Four design patterns (right column). The table lists: 1:1 Connection → Bridge, Builder, Mediator, State, Strategy, Visitor; 1:N Connection → Abstract Factory, Command, Flyweight, Iterator, Observer, Prototype, Adapter, Proxy, Visitor; 1:1 Recursive Connection → Decorator; 1:N Recursive Connection → Composite, Interpreter, Visitor. It also shows Unification → Factory Method, Template Method; 1:1 Recursive Unification → Chain of Responsibility; 1:N Recursive Unification → None; and "No metapattern" → Facade, Memento, Singleton. The layout makes clear that most GOF patterns correspond to at least one structural metapattern (with Visitor appearing in multiple categories), while a few patterns do not map to any metapattern.

page13_img_2.png.title: Design patterns and their key roles for motif matching across releases
page13_img_2.png.description: The table maps ten GOF design patterns (left column) to the specific ‘‘key’’ roles (right column) the authors use to recognize the same pattern instance across releases. Examples include Abstract Factory → {abstract factory, abstract product}; Adapter → {target, adapter, adaptee}; Command → {invoker, command, client}; Composite → {composite, component}; Decorator → {component, decorator}; Observer → {subject, observer}; Prototype → {prototype}; State/Strategy → {state/strategy, context}; Template Method → {abstract class}; Visitor → {visitor, element}. In the study these listed roles must remain bound to the same class names in two consecutive releases for a motif to be counted as a stable (duplicate) pattern instance.

page15_img_1.png.title: Weighted effects coding example for template/hook/implementation roles
page15_img_1.png.description: A small table (seven classes C1–C7) illustrating how role membership is encoded for regression using weighted effects coding. The left side shows binary membership: TEMPLATE = {C1, C4, C6, C7} (4 classes), HOOK = {C2, C5} (2 classes), IMPLEMENTATION = {C3} (1 class). The right side shows the recoded predictors when TEMPLATE is chosen as the base: classes that play a role get a 1 in that role’s column (e.g. C2 has HOOK=1), while base-role classes receive the negative fractional codes −2/4 under the HOOK column and −1/4 under the IMPLEMENTATION column (these are −n_k/n_base left unreduced). This demonstrates the paper’s approach to avoid perfect collinearity (leave the base out of the model) and obtain interpretable coefficients that compare each role to the weighted mean of all classes in the pattern.

page7_img_2.png.title: Mapping of GOF design patterns to template/hook/implementation metapattern roles
page7_img_2.png.description: A three-column mapping table that assigns each listed Gang-of-Four design pattern to the corresponding metapattern roles: TEMPLATE (stable caller), HOOK (interface or base), and IMPLEMENTATION (concrete implementer). Patterns shown include Abstract Factory (Client → Factory → Concrete Factory / Client → Product → Concrete Product), Adapter (Client → Target → Adapter), Command (Invoker → Command → Concrete Command), Composite (Composite → Component → Leaf), Decorator (Decorator → Component → Concrete Component), Factory Method (Creator → Creator → Concrete Creator), Observer (Subject → Observer → Concrete Observer), Prototype (Client → Prototype → Concrete Prototype), State/Strategy (Context → State → Concrete State), Template Method (Abstract Class → Abstract Class → Concrete Class), and Visitor (Client/Object Structure → Visitor/Element → Concrete Visitor/Concrete Element). The table is the canonical mapping the paper uses to relate concrete design-pattern roles to the abstract metapattern roles (template, hook, implementation) for subsequent change‑proneness and size analyses.

page5_img_1.png.title: Metapattern structures: Connection, Recursive Connection, and Unification
page5_img_1.png.description: The figure presents three small UML-style schematics side-by-side labeled Connection Metapattern, Recursive Connection Metapattern, and Unification Metapattern, showing the canonical Template, Hook and Implementation roles and the key methods/fields. In the Connection example the Template class holds a field “Hook myHook” and a template() method that delegates to myHook->hook(); the Hook box declares hook() and an Implementation box provides the concrete hook() override. The Recursive Connection variant shows the Template participating in the Hook inheritance hierarchy (triangle) while still delegating to a hook instance (illustrating the 1:1 or 1:N recursive case) and an Implementation subclass provides hook(); the Unification diagram merges template and hook into a single Template/Hook class that exposes both template() and hook(), with an Implementation subclass overriding hook(). These diagrams summarize the structural (1:1 and 1:N) relations that underlie many design patterns such as State/Strategy and explain how template/hook decomposition enables varying implementations.

page16_img_1.png.title: JHotDraw regression table: pattern role significance and R^2 across models
page16_img_1.png.description: A rotated summary table of regression results for JHotDraw showing per-pattern models and their explanatory power (R^2) along with role significance. Rows enumerate design patterns (Adapter, Abstract Factory, Command, Composite, Decorator, Factory Method, Observer, Prototype, State/Strategy, Template Method, Visitor) and grouped metapatterns; columns are grouped by model type (Mv: release only; Mvr: release+roles; Mvrs: release+roles+size; Mvs: release+size; M_v→s: roles→size). For each model the table prints significance/direction symbols for template (T), hook (H), implementation (M), remaining roles (mr), multi-role indicators (2, N) and the model R^2; arrow symbols denote positive/negative effects at three p-value thresholds and dots/NS/NA indicate non‑significance or not applicable. The table makes two patterns clear: adding size (columns Mvrs/Mvs) increases R^2 substantially compared to role-only models, and many role coefficients lose significance or change sign when size is controlled for; classes playing more than two roles (N column) are consistently associated with increased change-proneness (upward arrows).

page17_img_1.png.title: Xerces‑J model summary: role significance and R² across models
page17_img_1.png.description: A rotated summary table (Table 7) for the Xerces‑J project showing regression results for many design patterns and metapatterns. Rows list patterns (e.g., Adapter, Abstract Factory, Observer, State/Strategy, Template Method, etc. and grouped metapatterns), and columns are grouped by models (Mv, Mvr, Mvrs, Mvs and a size-as-response column) with subcolumns for template (T), hook (H), implementation (M), remaining roles (mr), two-role (2), >2 roles (N) and R². Cells use arrow symbols to indicate the sign and significance of a role coefficient (↑/↓ for positive/negative significance with stronger arrows for smaller p‑values), dots for not significant, and NA/NS for not applicable or model not significant; R² values (shown in the rightmost subcolumn of each model group) range roughly from ~0.11 up to ~0.56. Visually the table illustrates the paper’s findings: many hook/template/implementation roles show significance in role-only models (Mvr) but lose significance once class size is added (Mvrs/Mvs), and models that include size explain much more variance (higher R²).

page18_img_1.png.title: Table 8 — Eclipse JDT: role significance and R² for regression models
page18_img_1.png.description: A rotated results table (Table 8) reporting regression outcomes for Eclipse JDT across several model variants: Mv (release only), Mvr (release+roles), Mvrs (release+roles+size) and Mvs (release+size). Rows list individual design patterns (Adapter, Abstract Factory, Command, Composite, Decorator, Factory Method, Observer, Prototype, State/Strategy, Template Method, Visitor) and groups of metapatterns detected by DeMIMA and Thex; columns show role predictors (T = template, H = hook, M = implementation, mr = remaining roles, 2 = two roles, N = >2 roles) and an R² value for each model. Each cell contains an arrow symbol encoding the sign and significance of the role coefficient (direction = whether classes playing that role change more or less; multiple arrow forms denote three significance levels) or a dot/NA/NS when not significant or not applicable. The numeric R² values show a small explanatory power for release-only models (Mv, ~0.02–0.07) and modest improvement when adding roles (Mvr, up to ~0.16), while models that include size (Mvrs and Mvs) have substantially larger R² (roughly 0.30–0.44); many role indicators become non-significant or change direction once size is included, and classes playing more than two roles (N) frequently show positive, significant effects.

page13_img_1.png.title: Pattern and role cardinality counts across three Java projects
page13_img_1.png.description: Table 3 lists, for each design pattern and for metapatterns, the number of detected motifs (#) and the counts of classes that play 1, 2, or >2 distinct roles, reported separately for JHotDraw, Xerces, and Eclipse JDT. Rows include GOF design patterns (Adapter, Abstract Factory, Command, Composite, Decorator, Factory Method, Observer, Prototype, State/Strategy, Template Method, Visitor), Ptidej-derived metapatterns (Connection, Recursive connection, Unification) and Thex metapatterns; “NA” marks patterns absent in a project. Notable entries include very large counts for Abstract Factory and Factory Method (e.g., Abstract Factory: JHotDraw #=1259 and Xerces #=2657, absent in Eclipse JDT; Factory Method: Eclipse JDT #=3285), and substantially more metapattern instances found by Thex than the embedded Ptidej extraction (e.g., Connection in Eclipse JDT: Ptidej #=1250 vs Thex #=3324). The table also shows many classes participate in multiple roles (non-zero counts in the “N” column), supporting the paper’s claim that role multiplicity and abundant simple patterns drive much of the observed pattern membership.
